questions.prompt: Put these steps of setting up your dev environment, per Lesson 2, in the correct order.
items: Download the Windows LTS installer from nodejs.org
Run the downloaded .msi installer and click through the setup wizard
Open a terminal and run node -v and npm -v to confirm the install worked
Use VS Code's own built-in terminal to run commands without leaving the editor
questions.explain: Lesson 2 walks through this exact order: download the LTS build (always LTS, not Current, for this course), run the installer with its default options, confirm both node and npm print version numbers in a terminal, then install VS Code and use its integrated terminal going forward.

questions.prompt: What does the typeof operator actually return when called on the value null?
options: "object"
"null"
"undefined"
"boolean"
"number"
"symbol"
questions.explain: typeof null returning "object" is a genuine, long-standing bug baked into JavaScript since 1995 that's never been fixed, because fixing it would break too much existing code on the web. Lesson 3 calls this out by name specifically so it doesn't look like a mistake the first time a developer hits it.
questions.distractorExplain: It's tempting to guess "null" since that's literally the value being checked, but typeof never returns that string for any value — the actual (famously quirky) answer for null is "object", not "null".

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about JavaScript's variable declarations and primitive types, per Lesson 3.
options: const should be your default choice; reach for let only when you genuinely need to reassign the variable later
var has looser scoping rules than let and const, which is why this course avoids it in new code
bigint exists because JavaScript's regular number type can't safely represent whole numbers past 2^53 - 1
typeof null correctly returns "null"
undefined and null mean exactly the same thing, with no real distinction between them
questions.explain: const is the stated default, with let reserved for genuine reassignment. var's looser scoping is exactly why this course never uses it in new code. bigint exists specifically because a regular number can't safely represent integers past 2^53 - 1, which wei amounts routinely exceed. typeof null actually returns "object", and undefined ("declared, no value assigned") and null ("intentionally no value") are explicitly distinct concepts, not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 5, a function with no return statement doesn't return nothing — it returns ________, every time, silently.
questions.explain: A function that never hits a return statement still returns a value — specifically undefined — rather than returning "nothing." Lesson 5 flags this as one of the most common beginner surprises, since a value showing up as undefined unexpectedly is often a sign the function that produced it forgot to return.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 tool or concept to what it actually does, per Lessons 6-7.
right: Renders an array of objects as an actual readable table
Adds one more element to the end of an array
Returns undefined quietly, with no error thrown
Required when the property name is stored in a variable, instead of dot notation
questions.explain: .push() adds an element to the end of an array. Bracket notation is required when a property name lives in a variable (or has characters dot notation can't express). console.table renders an array of objects as an actual table instead of nested braces. Reading a missing property doesn't throw in JavaScript — it quietly returns undefined.

questions.prompt: What does this code actually print, and why, per Lesson 8?
options: 2, then a ReferenceError — because var leaks out of the if block (function-scoped) while let stays inside it (block-scoped)
2, then 1 — because both var and let leak out of the if block identically
A ReferenceError on the very first console.log, since neither variable exists outside the block
undefined, then undefined — both variables are hoisted but never assigned outside the block
questions.explain: var is scoped to the nearest function, so it leaks out of the if block and console.log(y) prints 2. let is scoped to the nearest block ({ }), so it never exists outside the if block at all, and console.log(x) throws a ReferenceError. This is the precise, concrete reason let/const replaced var.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an arrow function written with a single expression body and no braces, like (n) => n * 2, has an implicit ________ — whatever the expression evaluates to is automatically sent back as the result.
questions.explain: With no { } body, an arrow function's single expression is automatically returned without writing the return keyword at all — this is the implicit return shorthand Lesson 9 covers, and it shows up constantly in real code, especially as an argument passed to another function.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ES module (import/export) syntax, per Lesson 11.
options: A single file can have exactly one default export
A named import must use the exact exported name, or be renamed with as
CommonJS's require loads modules asynchronously, while ES modules load synchronously
Node.js needs either "type": "module" in package.json or a .mjs extension to treat files as ES modules
A default export is imported using curly braces, the same as a named export
questions.explain: A file can have exactly one default export, and a named import must match the exported name (or use as to rename it). Node.js decides CommonJS vs. ES modules based on package.json's "type" field or the .mjs/.cjs extension. CommonJS actually loads synchronously at runtime, not asynchronously — the statement has it backwards. A default import doesn't use curly braces at all; that's the whole point of a default export.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 12's chaining example over a list of transactions, put these three array-method steps in the order they're applied.
items: Filter out transactions with a zero value
Map each remaining transaction down to just its value
Reduce the values into a single running total
questions.explain: Lesson 12's chaining pattern runs filter first to narrow down to what matters, then map to pull out just the field needed, then reduce to collapse everything into one final total — exactly the order real blockchain code uses to summarize on-chain data.

questions.prompt: Which of these, per Lesson 13, correctly uses the rest operator (not the spread operator)?
options: function sum(...numbers) { return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0); }
const extended = [...base, 4, 5];
const updated = { ...wallet, balance: 250n };
shout`hello ${name}`;
questions.explain: ...numbers in a function's parameter list is the rest operator: it gathers any number of individual arguments into one real array. The other two use the identical ... syntax to spread an existing array or object's contents out, in place, inside a new literal — the opposite job. The last option is an unrelated tagged template.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 16, what are the three possible states of a Promise?
options: Pending, fulfilled, and rejected
Pending, resolved, and cancelled
Waiting, success, and error
Created, running, and finished
Open, closed, and settled
Queued, active, and complete
questions.explain: A Promise moves from pending to exactly one of fulfilled (succeeded, holding a resolved value) or rejected (failed, holding a reason) — and once it settles into either, it can never change state again.
questions.distractorExplain: "Resolved" and "cancelled" sound plausible, but they aren't the actual terms: "resolved" is loose colloquial language for fulfilled, and JavaScript Promises have no built-in "cancelled" state at all. The three real states are pending, fulfilled, and rejected.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the event loop, per Lesson 14.
options: setTimeout(fn, 0) still waits for every currently-running line of synchronous code to finish first
The microtask queue (resolved Promise callbacks) is fully drained before the event loop takes even one task off the regular task queue
JavaScript can run two pieces of your own code on separate threads at the same time
A single long-running synchronous function blocks timers, network callbacks, and rendering until it finishes
Web APIs like setTimeout and fetch run inside the same single call stack as your JavaScript code
questions.explain: Even a 0ms setTimeout never runs until the call stack is empty. The event loop always fully drains the microtask queue before taking even one task off the regular task queue, which is why a Promise callback beats a setTimeout scheduled first. JavaScript is single-threaded, so there's no true parallel execution of your own code. Web APIs run outside the JS engine entirely, not inside the call stack — that's the whole reason async work doesn't block it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in Node's error-first callback convention, the first parameter passed to the callback is always a(n) ________ (or null if none occurred).
questions.explain: Node's built-in APIs standardized on error-first callbacks: the first parameter is always an error, or null if nothing went wrong, and the second is the actual result. Checking that first parameter before touching the result is the rule, not the exception.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 19's getEthPrice example, put these steps of fetching and safely handling an API response in the correct order.
items: await fetch(url) to get the Response object
Check response.ok, and throw an error yourself if it's false
await response.json() to parse the body
Return the parsed value to the caller
questions.explain: fetch() resolves once the status and headers arrive, but checking response.ok has to happen before trusting the body, since fetch() doesn't reject on a 404 or 500 by itself. Only after confirming the response is actually OK does the example await response.json() to parse the body, then return the value to the caller.

questions.prompt: An async function rejects, with no try/catch anywhere inside it and no .catch() on the call. What actually happens, per Lesson 18?
options: In modern Node.js, the unhandled promise rejection crashes the process
The rejection is silently ignored and the program continues normally
JavaScript automatically retries the failed operation up to three times
The program pauses indefinitely, waiting for the promise to be manually resolved
questions.explain: With no try/catch and no .catch() anywhere, a rejection has nowhere to go. Lesson 18 is explicit that in modern Node.js an unhandled promise rejection crashes the process — this is never silent in practice, only in the moment the code was written without handling it.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 20, which statement best describes what TypeScript actually is?
options: A superset of JavaScript — nearly every valid JS file is already close to valid TypeScript, with the types erased entirely once it compiles down to .js
An entirely separate programming language that merely resembles JavaScript
A JavaScript framework specifically for building user interfaces
A runtime library that must ship to the browser so it can check types while the page is running
questions.explain: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript: you write the same JavaScript syntax plus optional type annotations, tsc checks those types, and then compiles to plain .js with every type annotation erased — browsers and Node only ever run the resulting JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about any and unknown in TypeScript, per Lesson 21.
options: any turns off type checking entirely for that value
unknown also accepts any value, but forces you to narrow it before you're allowed to use it
unknown is generally the safer choice to reach for instead of any
any and unknown behave identically in every situation
A variable typed unknown can have any of its methods called directly, with no checks required
questions.explain: any quietly defeats the point of using TypeScript by turning off checking entirely. unknown accepts any value too, but the compiler blocks you from using it until you narrow its actual type first — which is exactly why the lesson recommends preferring unknown whenever any looks tempting. Calling a method directly on an unknown value is a compiler error, not something that just works.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: declaring the same interface name twice causes TypeScript to combine the two declarations' members into one — per Lesson 22, this is called declaration ________.
questions.explain: Declaration merging is interface's one real structural edge over type: re-declaring the same interface name merges its members together, which is useful for extending a type from a library. Attempting the same thing with type is a compiler error.

questions.prompt: Match each TypeScript narrowing tool to what it actually narrows, per Lesson 25.
left: A discriminated union's shared literal field
right: Narrows class instances, like checking for Error
Narrows the entire object from one shared tag, like status
Confirms specifically that a value is an array
questions.explain: typeof only covers primitives. instanceof narrows class instances, like Error. Array.isArray confirms specifically that a value is an array, since typeof unhelpfully returns "object" for arrays too. A discriminated union's shared literal field (like status) narrows the entire object from one check, not just that one field.

questions.prompt: What is the inferred type of n, per Lesson 24?
options: number — TypeScript infers T from the argument passed at this specific call site
any — generics always erase the type information back to any
T — the literal, unresolved placeholder
unknown — TypeScript refuses to infer a type parameter automatically
questions.explain: T is a placeholder filled in per call. Passing [1, 2, 3] lets TypeScript infer T as number for this call, with no manual annotation required, so n comes back correctly typed number — exactly the type information a plain any[] version of this function would have thrown away.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 29, what happens if tsconfig's target is set to ES2017 or lower in a project whose code uses bigint literals like 2_500_000_000_000_000_000n?
options: The compiler rejects every one of those literals with an error, even though the bigint type itself has existed since TS 3.2
The code compiles fine, but every bigint value silently becomes a regular number at runtime
Declaring a bigint still works; only arithmetic on it fails to compile
TypeScript automatically upgrades the target to ES2020 behind the scenes
questions.explain: bigint literals specifically require target ES2020 or newer. Setting target to ES2017 or lower causes the compiler to reject every bigint literal with an error — a fact worth knowing since bigint the type has existed since TS 3.2, even though literals need the newer target.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ethers.js v6 and viem, per Lesson 27.
options: Both libraries use native bigint for on-chain amounts like balances and gas values
ethers v6 dropped the custom BigNumber class that existed in ethers v5
viem is class-based, requiring new PublicClient() to create a client
A WalletClient in viem is built from an account, not a Signer object
ethers' Contract class and viem's readContract function use identical call syntax
questions.explain: Both libraries agree on native bigint for on-chain amounts — that debate is settled. ethers v6 dropped the old BigNumber class from v5. viem is functional, not class-based: it builds clients with factory functions like createPublicClient, never new. A WalletClient is explicitly built from an account, unlike ethers' Signer. The two libraries' contract-call syntax (method-call style vs. an explicit readContract function) is a real, named difference, not identical.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 28, declaring an ABI array with ________ turns it into a literal type the compiler can read function-by-function, letting viem narrow functionName and infer argument/return types automatically.
questions.explain: A plain abi: Abi array type-checks structurally but doesn't let the compiler distinguish which function names and argument types are actually valid. Declaring the ABI with as const locks it to its exact literal shape, which is what lets readContract narrow functionName and infer types with no manual generics.

questions.prompt: Put these tsconfig.json concerns in the order Lesson 29 addresses them.
items: Set target to ES2022 so bigint literals compile
Set module and moduleResolution to NodeNext for ESM-only web3 packages
Enable strict mode for checks like strictNullChecks and noImplicitAny
Add skipLibCheck so a bad dependency's .d.ts doesn't block the build
questions.explain: Lesson 29 walks through its minimal tsconfig.json in exactly this order: target first (required the moment bigint literals are used), then module/moduleResolution (where ESM-only web3 packages actually break), then strict mode's most valuable flags, then skipLibCheck and resolveJsonModule as the last two settings.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 30, why is validating process.env with a zod schema better than trusting process.env directly?
options: process.env values are typed string | undefined regardless of whether the .env file actually has them set, so an unvalidated missing variable turns into undefined deep inside a provider constructor instead of failing at startup with a clear message
TypeScript cannot read process.env at all without a zod schema present
zod automatically converts every environment variable into a bigint
process.env values are encrypted by default, and zod is required to decrypt them
questions.explain: process.env.RPC_URL is always typed string | undefined, whether or not it's actually set. Validating it once with a zod schema at startup means a missing or malformed variable crashes immediately with a clear message, instead of silently becoming undefined three function calls deep inside a provider constructor.

questions.prompt: Running node check-balance.js 0xABC..., what does process.argv[2] actually contain, per Lesson 33?
options: "0xABC..." — the first real command-line argument typed after the script name
The path to the Node executable
The path to the script file itself
undefined, since process.argv only ever has two elements
questions.explain: process.argv[0] is the Node executable path and process.argv[1] is the script path — real arguments only start at index 2. For node check-balance.js 0xABC..., process.argv[2] is the string "0xABC...".

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about npm and package.json, per Lesson 32.
options: devDependencies are only needed while building or developing, like a TypeScript compiler
npm install --omit=dev skips devDependencies, which is exactly what a deployment pipeline should do
The caret (^) range allows new minor and patch versions, but not a new major version
package-lock.json should generally not be committed to the repository
npx runs a package's CLI without requiring a permanent global install
questions.explain: devDependencies (like typescript) are only needed while building; --omit=dev is exactly what a production deploy should use to skip them. ^6.13.0 allows new minor/patch versions up to but not including 7.0.0 — a new major is excluded. npx runs a CLI tool on demand with no permanent global install. package-lock.json should be committed, not excluded — it records the exact installed versions so two developers don't silently end up on different versions of the same ^ range.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 6 file-system/server concept to what it actually does, per Lessons 35-36.
right: Values captured from :segments in a route's path
Builds a file path using the correct separator for the current OS
Returns a Buffer unless a "utf-8" encoding argument is passed
A 4-argument app.use() registered last, catching errors passed via next(err)
questions.explain: readFile returns a raw Buffer unless you pass "utf-8" as the encoding, in which case it returns a plain string. path.join picks the correct separator for whatever OS the script actually runs on. Express recognizes error-handling middleware by its four arguments, and it must be registered last. req.params holds whatever values were captured from :segments in the route path.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 38, put these chain-reader capstone files in the order they're built and explained.
items: chain.ts — typed provider wrapper returning Result<T>
index.ts — the main() entry point tying both together
questions.explain: Lesson 38 builds the capstone bottom-up: config.ts first (so RPC_URL is validated before anything else runs), then chain.ts (the typed read logic that depends on that config), and finally index.ts (the thin entry point that calls chain.ts and decides what to print and which exit code to use).

questions.prompt: Per the capstone's definition of done in Lesson 37, what should happen when chain-reader is run with a malformed address or an invalid RPC_URL?
options: It prints a clear error and exits with a non-zero code, never throwing a raw unhandled stack trace
It silently ignores the bad input and prints the balance of a default address instead
It crashes with an unhandled stack trace, which is the expected behavior for a CLI tool
It automatically retries against a different public RPC endpoint until one works
questions.explain: The capstone's definition of done is explicit: running it with a malformed address or an invalid RPC_URL prints a clear error and exits with a non-zero code — it never throws a raw, unhandled stack trace. This is the direct payoff of Chapters 5 and 6's Result<T> and exit-code patterns, proven end to end.
